name: Microneedling pen (electric)
lead: An electric microneedling pen is a motorised handheld device that drives a cartridge of fine needles rapidly up and down into the skin to create controlled micro-injuries. It is used for acne scars, skin texture, stretch marks, pigmentation disorders and hair thinning, and is a staple of skin and scar discussion in looksmaxxing forums; the Dermapen is the best-known branded example [10][2][21].

Dermatology research on microneedling, including pen devices, consists largely of small trials, many from single centres, that compare it with peels or other treatments or use it to deliver topical products and platelet-rich plasma. A systematic review of 51 articles and 1,029 patients described microneedling as a relatively safe procedure [1]. Rare but notable adverse reactions have been reported, including granulomatous reactions in which motorized pens and topical vitamin C application were implicated in most published cases [3].

paras: Pen devices hold a disposable needle cartridge and move the needles in and out of the skin at adjustable speed and depth. Their vertical stamping motion is contrasted by manufacturers with the angled entry of rolling devices [21]. According to Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, the Dermapen was introduced in 2010 by the Australian company DermapenWorld and has gone through several generations, including a fourth-generation model launched in 2018 [21]. That account relies largely on manufacturer-sourced material.
Cheaper generic pens and cartridges are sold to consumers online; looksmax.org discussions compare them with clinical devices [11][12].

Reviews describe microneedling as creating micro-injuries that start inflammation, proliferation and remodeling phases, activate platelet growth factors and stimulate fibroblasts to produce collagen and elastin [2]. The puncture channels are also reported to increase penetration of topical agents [2].

A randomized comparison of 60 patients with atrophic acne scars found that a pen-based microneedling group improved more than a Jessner's peel group, and that combining the two gave the best results [5]. Other studies compared a pen with glycolic acid peels for acne scars [15], assessed two microneedle devices on opposite sides of the face [10], and compared microneedling with plasma regeneration for stretch marks [13].

Pens have also been studied as delivery tools in melasma with platelet-rich plasma [4] or tranexamic acid versus vitamin C [16], in vitiligo with topical drugs [8][9][18], and in androgenetic alopecia with platelet-rich plasma [7]. Many of these are small, regionally conducted studies, and a review lists conditions where benefit has been reported while noting the heterogeneity of methods [2].

Human trials have studied pen-type microneedling for acne scars [5][15][10], stretch marks [13], melasma [4][16], vitiligo [8][9][18] and androgenetic alopecia [7], mostly as small comparative or randomized studies. A systematic review of 51 articles covering 1,029 patients evaluated safety across device types [1]. Strong trial evidence of long-term durability was not found.

A systematic review of microneedling adverse effects covering roller, stamp, pen and radiofrequency devices examined published complications [1]. Rare granulomatous reactions have been described in 15 patients, with motorized pen use and topical vitamin C implicated in most cases; the authors note that these can be treatment-resistant [3].
Because needles break the skin barrier, products applied afterward can enter deeper tissue than intended, a point discussed in the reviews of reactions [1][3].

On looksmax.org, members ask what maximum needle depth is appropriate on the face for a pen, with replies describing depths of 1 to 2 mm, intervals between sessions, and waiting periods before reintroducing actives such as vitamin C, tretinoin and acids; some replies suggest paying for professional radiofrequency microneedling instead [11]. Other threads discuss cheap generic pens, with one user reporting more than two years of use [12]. These are personal reports, not clinical advice.

timeline.event: Dermapen introduced as the first automated microneedling pen, per its maker [21]

lore.intro: Electric pens are discussed on looksmax.org as a home or low-cost route to skin renewal, with attention to needle depth and device choice.

claims.claim: Deeper needle depth gives better results, with limits around 1.5 mm
claims.believers: Posters say deeper is generally better but that 1.5-2 mm should be used rarely, risks scarring, and needs longer breaks from actives [11].
claims.experts: Published studies use varied depths and devices; reviews describe serious adverse effects, including granulomatous reactions, as uncommon [1][3].

claims.claim: Cheap generic pens work as well as branded ones
claims.believers: One poster reports a generic pen working well after two years of heavy use, while another recommends a different type [12].
claims.experts: A study compared two microneedle devices on opposite sides of the face for acne scars [10]; no study of low-cost consumer pens against branded devices was found.

card.summary: Motorised needle pen for collagen induction; decent small-trial support for scars and texture, but rare reactions and depth/hygiene issues at home.
card.note: Rare granulomatous reactions reported, mostly with motorized pens and topical vitamin C.

quick.overview:
An electric microneedling pen rapidly punctures the skin with fine disposable needles to trigger repair. It is used for acne scars, texture, stretch marks and sometimes hair or pigment problems, and is a staple of looksmax skincare talk.

Small randomized studies report improvement in acne scars, often better when combined with peels or other agents, but many trials are small and from single centres, and long-term data are limited.
quick.mechanism: The needles create micro-injuries that start wound healing, release growth factors and stimulate collagen and elastin production, and the channels may help topical products penetrate.
quick.risks: A systematic review described microneedling as relatively safe overall. Rare granulomatous reactions have been reported, with motorized pens and topical vitamin C implicated in most cases. Forum discussions of deep home settings are personal reports rather than clinical guidance.
